rationale: Start with a broad gradient at intermediate temperature to locate the elution window for all 10 compounds and identify critical pairs. This provides a baseline for targeted gradient trimming and temperature optimization.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while measuring how the critical pairs respond to slope. The baseline has substantial resolution margin, so a faster gradient may retain full separation.

Keep the fast gradient and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the crowded middle cluster. This should shorten retention while revealing whether temperature can rescue the critical pair without a longer gradient.

Use a slightly shallower gradient to improve middle-cluster resolution, with temperature just below 60 C to move away from the new co-elution. The higher temperature should offset much of the added gradient time.

Injection 4 has already reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the best method. Test a modestly higher starting organic fraction to seek another maximum-scoring method with improved resolution margins while keeping early peaks retained.

Retain injection 4 as the maximum-scoring method and test a slightly shallower gradient at the same temperature and starting composition. This may increase the narrow resolution margins while keeping the last peak near the zero-time-penalty window.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test the unexplored low-temperature selectivity regime with the faster gradient. Cooling may separate the middle-cluster pair that was critical at 40 C while keeping the last peak near the zero-time-penalty window.

Test a 5 C decrease from the best method to map local temperature sensitivity without changing the gradient. This will show whether the two marginally resolved pairs at 55 C can gain separation margin while preserving a short run.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction moves the 60 C critical pair apart on the opposite side of its co-elution. This explores a faster alternative while retaining injection 4 as the established maximum-scoring method.

Shorten injection 9’s gradient to test whether greater steepness further separates the pair that crossed near 60 C. This could produce a faster maximum-scoring alternative, though the neighboring pair may lose resolution.

Increase the starting organic fraction one grid step from injection 9 to test further improvement of its critical pair, using the longer gradient to protect neighboring separations. Monitor the first two peaks closely because their retention and resolution may become limiting.

Return to the maximum-scoring region and slightly flatten injection 5’s gradient to improve its sole deficient pair. Combining this slope with the higher starting fraction may balance both critical pairs above 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 8 minutes.

Flatten injection 12’s gradient one more step to lift its R = 1.47 pair above baseline resolution. The other critical pair appears relatively slope-insensitive, and the predicted last retention time is close to 8 minutes.

Trim injection 13’s gradient endpoint while preserving its slope exactly, since the last peak eluted near organic fraction 0.56. All peaks should remain within the gradient, preserving the maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient and lower final organic fraction.

Use a gradient slope between injections 12 and 13 to balance their critical-pair resolutions. This should preserve full resolution while moving the last peak below 8 minutes, adding time margin to the maximum-scoring region.

Test whether a higher starting fraction combined with a shallower slope can improve the balance between the two critical pairs. The higher start should offset some added retention from the shallower gradient, potentially preserving the zero time penalty.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 13 to assess whether its resolution margin improves further. The last peak may slightly exceed the zero-time-penalty window, so retain the established CRF 1.000 methods unless this offers a useful separation advantage.

Flatten injection 16’s gradient to improve its sole deficient pair while retaining its stronger separation of the other critical pair. This tests whether increased resolution margin can be achieved without a substantial time penalty; the maximum CRF is already secured.

Reduce the slope modestly from injection 18 to bring its R = 1.41 pair above 1.5 while preserving the other critical pair’s margin. The projected last peak is near 9 minutes, testing a potentially better-resolved alternative at the edge of the zero-time-penalty region.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 17 within the confirmed zero-time-penalty window of approximately 9 minutes. This should strengthen the earlier critical pair while checking that the relatively slope-insensitive later pair remains above 1.5.

Complete the local temperature comparison around injection 4 by testing 60 C at the same gradient slope. This will quantify the upper-temperature selectivity boundary while retaining the established CRF 1.000 methods.

Stay at the successful 55 C temperature and test a slightly shallower slope than injection 20. This should preserve baseline resolution and keep the last peak below approximately 9 minutes, further defining the maximum-scoring operating window.
Test a trimmed gradient with slope between the successful injections 17 and 20. It should keep all peaks within the gradient and preserve CRF 1.000, with the last peak expected near 8.3 minutes.

Test a slope just shallower than injection 6 with a trimmed endpoint that remains above the elution window. This probes the resolution boundary near the established maximum-scoring region while keeping all compounds comfortably within acquisition time.

For the final injection, trim the endpoint while preserving injection 4’s starting composition, temperature, and exact gradient slope. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, reproducing the maximum CRF of 1.000 with a shorter programmed gradient.
